newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss aid foundation may end Holocaust row.
newsitem.headline: Swiss aid foundation may end Holocaust row.

text.p: Switzerland's surprise offer to create a huge humanitarian foundation is a bold move that could finally bury a damaging crisis over the Swiss role in World War Two, diplomats and commentators said on Thursday.

Most Swiss commentators praised the human rights foundation unveiled on Wednesday as a return to the moral high ground after months of battering on the world stage from critics who claimed Switzerland abused its neutrality to profit from the war.
"The 'good Swiss' are to be resurrected," the country's biggest newspaper, the tabloid Blick, said in a commentary on the proposal by President Arnold Koller.

Koller surprised parliament and voters -- who will probably take the final decision in a referendum -- by proposing a "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" funded by seven billion Swiss francs ($4.7 billion) in official gold reserves and aimed at aiding foreign and domestic victims of the Holocaust and other human rights abuses.

The conservative Neue Zuercher Zeitung (NZZ) said the Swiss government had finally broken out of its defensive mood with a forward-looking project that proved Swiss solidarity with victims of the Holocaust and other atrocities.
"Switzerland has a good, but at the moment contested, reputation as a humanitarian state to lose -- or to confirm in a new and stronger form," the NZZ wrote.

Switzerland can use its new momentum to handle critics led by the New York-based World Jewish Congress (WJC) and its political allies when Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti visits the United States March 11-14.
"Cotti is going to the U.S. to present the Swiss position on its efforts in connection with the Swiss role in World War Two," a foreign ministry spokesman said.

Special ambassador Thomas Borer, head of a Berne task force coordinating the response to attacks, said the proposed foundation should end one of Switzerland's worst foreign policy crises by convincing its critics of Swiss goodwill.

"I expect our foreign critics to recognise Switzerland's unprecedented efforts favourably, both in coming to grips with its history and in making humanitarian gestures, and to treat us fairly," Borer told Reuters.

"The worst effects of the crisis have been overcome," he said, referring to a new spirit of cooperation between the Swiss and the WJC launched in the past month after more than a year of increasingly bitter quarrelling.
The new cooperation was made possible after the three biggest Swiss banks donated 100 million Swiss francs last month to set up a Holocaust memorial fund to be run by Berne and major Jewish groups.

The Swiss government proposal on Wednesday also included another donation of 100 million Swiss francs from the Swiss National Bank (SNB) to the rapid relief fund for needy Holocaust survivors and their families.

The Swiss effort to defuse international criticism also includes two commissions set up last year, one to comb Swiss bank records for accounts left by Holocaust victims and another to make a sweeping probe of the Swiss wartime financial role.

Borer said it was always possible controversy could erupt again over the Swiss role as a wartime financial centre open to all sides, including Hitler's Germany and its fascist allies who surrounded the small Alpine state for most of the war.
"But I am confident that these major steps we have taken will allow a factual and constructive cooperation, with no return to polemics," he added.
